2:165.ar: وَمِنَ ٱلنَّاسِ مَن يَتَّخِذُ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ أَندَادࣰ ا يُحِبُّونَهُمۡ كَحُبِّ ٱللَّهِۖ وَٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓاْ أَشَدُّ حُبࣰّ ا لِّلَّهِۗ وَلَوۡ يَرَى ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوٓاْ إِذۡ يَرَوۡنَ ٱلۡعَذَابَ أَنَّ ٱلۡقُوَّةَ لِلَّهِ جَمِيعࣰ ا وَأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ شَدِيدُ ٱلۡعَذَابِ
2:165.en: Yet of mankind are some who take unto themselves (objects of worship which they set as) rivals to Allah, loving them with a love like (that which is the due) of Allah (only) - those who believe are stauncher in their love for Allah - Oh, that those who do evil had but known, (on the day) when they behold the doom, that power belongeth wholly to Allah, and that Allah is severe in punishment

87:8.en: And We shall ease thy way unto the state of ease

3:35.ar: إِذۡ قَالَتِ ٱمۡرَأَتُ عِمۡرَٰنَ رَبِّ إِنِّي نَذَرۡتُ لَكَ مَا فِي بَطۡنِي مُحَرَّرࣰ ا فَتَقَبَّلۡ مِنِّيٓۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلۡعَلِيمُ
3:35.en: (Remember) when the wife of 'Imran said: My Lord! I have vowed unto Thee that which is in my belly as a consecrated (offering). Accept it from me. Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Hearer, the Knower

3:36.ar: فَلَمَّا وَضَعَتۡهَا قَالَتۡ رَبِّ إِنِّي وَضَعۡتُهَآ أُنثَىٰ وَٱللَّهُ أَعۡلَمُ بِمَا وَضَعَتۡ وَلَيۡسَ ٱلذَّكَرُ كَٱلۡأُنثَىٰۖ وَإِنِّي سَمَّيۡتُهَا مَرۡيَمَ وَإِنِّيٓ أُعِيذُهَا بِكَ وَذُرِّيَّتَهَا مِنَ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنِ ٱلرَّجِيمِ
3:36.en: And when she was delivered she said: My Lord! Lo! I am delivered of a female - Allah knew best of what she was delivered - the male is not as the female; and lo! I have named her Mary, and lo! I crave Thy protection for her and for her offspring from Satan the outcast

12:84.ar: وَتَوَلَّىٰ عَنۡهُمۡ وَقَالَ يَٰٓأَسَفَىٰ عَلَىٰ يُوسُفَ وَٱبۡيَضَّتۡ عَيۡنَاهُ مِنَ ٱلۡحُزۡنِ فَهُوَ كَظِيمࣱ‏
12:84.en: And he turned away from them and said: Alas, my grief for Joseph! And his eyes were whitened with the sorrow that he was suppressing

12:85.ar: قَالُواْ تَٱللَّهِ تَفۡتَؤُاْ تَذۡكُرُ يُوسُفَ حَتَّىٰ تَكُونَ حَرَضًا أَوۡ تَكُونَ مِنَ ٱلۡهَٰلِكِينَ
12:85.en: They said: By Allah, thou wilt never cease remembering Joseph till thy health is ruined or thou art of those who perish

12:86.ar: قَالَ إِنَّمَآ أَشۡكُواْ بَثِّي وَحُزۡنِيٓ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ وَأَعۡلَمُ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ مَا لَا تَعۡلَمُونَ
12:86.en: He said: I expose my distress and anguish only unto Allah, and I know from Allah that which ye know not

DHPiiUB-b48.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah: The Rituals, Episode 19
DHPiiUB-b48.one_line: How the first three postures of salah cure aimlessness, showing off and vanity, and how sujud teaches desperate, honest dua.
DHPiiUB-b48.summary: Salah is divided in half: the first three postures are offerings to Allah, the rest is asking, and the more one invests first, the more one gains after, as with any audience before a great person. He then shows what each offering cures. The recitation, built around the request for guidance, cures aimlessness, the root of the heart's diseases and of much depression and anxiety; a Muslim cannot be bored, and should read the Quran until he finds the cause he will live for. Magnification in ruku cures ostentation, because people's eyes only matter when Allah is not great enough in our hearts. Praise on rising cures vanity by turning the spotlight from oneself to Allah, while we should credit others generously. Sujud is the most awkward and humble posture, once used by people pleading for their lives; a Muslim gives it to no one but Allah and never grovels to a human, a fearlessness of death the early Arabs carried. Since Allah's deal with us is so tilted in our favour, dua should be desperate, not formal. He asks people to drop their social masks and speak to Allah as the needy servant they really are, citing Maryam's mother and Ya'qub.

outline.heading: Salah tips and postures that mirror the soul
outline.gist: The heart's diseases together lower the quality of salah; while tazkiyah works, the tips help, and each posture and transition reflects a spiritual one.

outline.heading: Two halves: offering before asking
outline.gist: The first three movements are what you offer Allah and the rest is your request; as when meeting someone of status, you establish the relationship before asking.

outline.heading: Review of the three offerings
outline.gist: Reciting His guidance shows commitment to the straight path, ruku gives your opinion of Allah, and rising shows the attitude of praise and gratitude.

outline.heading: Standing cures aimlessness
outline.gist: Al-Fatihah's request for guidance treats the disease of living without direction, like a game character wandering while the clock runs out.

outline.heading: The unanswered existential question
outline.gist: Much depression and anxiety stem from never answering why we exist, with consequences cascading from it; longer recitation better establishes purpose.

outline.heading: A Muslim cannot be bored
outline.gist: There is so much work for humanity, the planet and the oppressed that boredom and Islam cannot coexist; guidance is the root of all good.

outline.heading: Ruku cures ostentation
outline.gist: Showing off exists because Allah is not great enough in the heart, so we need others watching too and take equals beside Him.

outline.heading: Allah is free of need of partners
outline.gist: In the narration Allah leaves a deed shared with another to that partner; magnifying Him is the antidote to needing people's validation.

outline.heading: Seeking feedback versus seeking approval
outline.gist: Wanting to know if a lesson helped is good, but the intention is pleasing Allah; aimlessness comes before the other diseases of the heart.

outline.heading: Purpose weakens every disease of the heart
outline.gist: Even non-Muslims devoted to a cause, like a scientist absorbed in research, often show admirable humility; aimless people cannot shake their diseases.

outline.heading: Read the Quran until you find your cause
outline.gist: Find a command to live by, such as justice, caring for orphans or education, using your passion and expertise; then no one's gaze rivals Allah's.

outline.heading: Rising from ruku cures vanity
outline.gist: Vanity is shining the spotlight on yourself and crediting yourself; aimless people need it to feel any value.

outline.heading: Allah decides who deserves praise
outline.gist: Much of what we achieve came from upbringing, mentors and gifts; we are not the main character, so praise goes to Him and failures to ourselves.

outline.heading: Credit others, not yourself
outline.gist: With good assumptions we should praise others' work, but we have reversed the ethic, claiming credit for ourselves and discrediting everyone else.

outline.heading: The three cures, then the open buffet
outline.gist: Done properly, the first half rids you of aimlessness, ostentation and vanity and earns the unscripted second half.

outline.heading: Sujud: the most humble posture
outline.gist: An awkward position no one offers anyone, historically used by people pleading for their lives before a king.

outline.heading: Never grovel before a human
outline.gist: Even facing execution a Muslim holds his head high, because only Allah gave the life and decides when it ends; others merely hold the gun for now.

outline.heading: Why the Arabs received the message: no fear of death
outline.gist: They were raised to seek an honourable death; Khalid ibn al-Walid wept at dying in bed until reminded of the reward of martyrdom for the sincere. Consumerism has made death our biggest fear.

outline.heading: Dying while doing your work for Allah
outline.gist: One of his teachers died mid-lesson, as he had asked; find what you want to die doing for Allah's sake.

outline.heading: Praise and magnification before asking
outline.gist: In sujud you ask from utter poverty; its short glorification serves as the praise that should precede any dua.

outline.heading: Sujud as the best place for dua
outline.gist: The Prophet urged abundant dua in prostration; even outside prayer he raised his hands high with head lowered in humility.

outline.heading: A deal rigged in our favour
outline.gist: Allah gives a way of life that helps only us, then rewards us for following it; such a deal leaves nothing fitting but humble pleading.

outline.heading: Dua is desperation, not formality
outline.gist: Dignity belongs with peers, but before Allah it is out of place; speaking to Him like a business meeting misreads the relationship.

outline.heading: Take off the social mask
outline.gist: His exercise of making dua a second time without repeating anything leaves people blank, because they speak to Allah as doctor or parent; self-honesty lets you speak as the needy sinner you are.

outline.heading: The Prophet's dua
outline.gist: He loved dua and kept it general, too humble to presume he knew what was good for him, except rare cases like the battle when the believers might be wiped out.

outline.heading: The tone of a face on the ground; a daughter's mistake
outline.gist: Let the attitude match the posture; a beloved daughter who shamed her father pleads with both embarrassment and love.

outline.heading: A son returning to his mother
outline.gist: A son who abandoned his mother for years returns pleading at her feet, trusting her love; every sujud is such a return to Allah.

outline.heading: Keep the line open beyond Ramadan
outline.gist: Ramadan is a yearly workshop in dua that people forget afterwards; keep the conversation going all year.

outline.heading: The mother of Maryam speaking to Allah
outline.gist: She dedicated her child, then told Allah it was a girl, explaining her heart though He knew; she was used to talking to Him.

outline.heading: Ya'qub complains only to Allah
outline.gist: Blind from decades of grief, he told his sons he complained of his sorrow to Allah alone and knew from Him what they did not.

themes.label: Salah: its meaning, etiquette and significance
themes.note: The two halves of salah and what each of the first three postures offers.

themes.label: Purpose, meaning and the point of life
themes.note: Aimlessness is the root disease; recitation and the request for guidance establish purpose, and a Muslim cannot be bored.

themes.label: Intention and sincerity (niyyah, ikhlas)
themes.note: Magnifying Allah is the cure for ostentation and the need for people's validation.

themes.label: Humility vs vanity and arrogance
themes.note: Praise belongs to Allah; crediting oneself is vanity, while others should be credited.

themes.label: Courage and commitment
themes.note: Never grovel before people; the early Arabs' lack of fear of death and seeking an honourable end.

themes.label: Dua and invocation
themes.note: Sujud as the place of desperate, honest dua without social masks, illustrated by Maryam's mother and Ya'qub.

themes.label: Self-honesty and self-accountability (muhasabah)
themes.note: You must know who you really are to speak to Allah as that person.

quran.point: The request for guidance at the heart of every recitation, the cure for aimlessness.
Some take equals besides Allah and love them as they should love Him.
Allah eases the believer toward ultimate ease.
Maryam's mother dedicates her child and tells Allah she bore a girl, seeking refuge for her.
Ya'qub loses his sight from grief and complains only to Allah.

Allah says He is the most free of need of partners; whoever associates another in a deed, He leaves him with it.
Whoever sincerely asks for martyrdom is given its rank even if he dies in his bed.
The Prophet would go down into sujud quickly, as if falling.
Increase your dua in sujud, for it is most likely to be answered.
The Prophet raised his hands in dua until the whiteness of his armpits showed.
At Badr the Prophet pleaded that if this small band perished Allah would no longer be worshipped.

maxims: You cannot be Muslim and bored
Read the Quran until you find your cause
Aimlessness comes before every disease of the heart
Dua is the desperate speaking to the only one who can help
Self-dignity has no place before Allah
You are not the main character; Allah is

stories.who: Khalid ibn al-Walid on his deathbed
stories.point: He grieved at dying in bed rather than in battle; the early Arabs' fearlessness of death prepared them for Islam.

stories.who: The sheikh's teacher who died while teaching
stories.point: Ask to die doing the work you do for Allah.

stories.who: The mother of Maryam
stories.point: She spoke to Allah openly about her heart even though He knew it.

stories.who: Ya'qub grieving for Yusuf and Binyamin

contemporary: Consumerism making death our greatest fear
Depression and anxiety rooted in unanswered existential questions
takeaways: Spend real time in the first three postures before asking in sujud.

31:13.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ لُقۡمَٰنُ لِٱبۡنِهِۦ وَهُوَ يَعِظُهُۥ يَٰبُنَيَّ لَا تُشۡرِكۡ بِٱللَّهِۖ إِنَّ ٱلشِّرۡكَ لَظُلۡمٌ عَظِيمࣱ‏
31:13.en: And (remember) when Luqman said unto his son, when he was exhorting him: O my dear son! Ascribe no partners unto Allah. Lo! to ascribe partners (unto Him) is a tremendous wrong

31:14.ar: وَوَصَّيۡنَا ٱلۡإِنسَٰنَ بِوَٰلِدَيۡهِ حَمَلَتۡهُ أُمُّهُۥ وَهۡنًا عَلَىٰ وَهۡنࣲ وَفِصَٰلُهُۥ فِي عَامَيۡنِ أَنِ ٱشۡكُرۡ لِي وَلِوَٰلِدَيۡكَ إِلَيَّ ٱلۡمَصِيرُ
31:14.en: And We have enjoined upon man concerning his partners - His mother beareth him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years - Give thanks unto Me and unto thy parents. Unto Me is the journeying

31:15.ar: وَإِن جَٰهَدَاكَ عَلَىٰٓ أَن تُشۡرِكَ بِي مَا لَيۡسَ لَكَ بِهِۦ عِلۡمࣱ فَلَا تُطِعۡهُمَاۖ وَصَاحِبۡهُمَا فِي ٱلدُّنۡيَا مَعۡرُوفࣰ اۖ وَٱتَّبِعۡ سَبِيلَ مَنۡ أَنَابَ إِلَيَّۚ ثُمَّ إِلَيَّ مَرۡجِعُكُمۡ فَأُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا كُنتُمۡ تَعۡمَلُونَ
31:15.en: But if they strive with thee to make thee ascribe unto Me as partner that of which thou hast no knowledge, then obey them not. Consort with them in the world kindly, and follow the path of him who repenteth unto Me. Then unto Me will be your return, and I shall tell you what ye used to do

31:16.ar: يَٰبُنَيَّ إِنَّهَآ إِن تَكُ مِثۡقَالَ حَبَّةࣲ مِّنۡ خَرۡدَلࣲ فَتَكُن فِي صَخۡرَةٍ أَوۡ فِي ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ أَوۡ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ يَأۡتِ بِهَا ٱللَّهُۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَطِيفٌ خَبِيرࣱ‏
31:16.en: O my dear son! Lo! though it be but the weight of a grain of mustard-seed, and though it be in a rock, or in the heavens, or in the earth, Allah will bring it forth. Lo! Allah is Subtile, Aware

31:17.ar: يَٰبُنَيَّ أَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَأۡمُرۡ بِٱلۡمَعۡرُوفِ وَٱنۡهَ عَنِ ٱلۡمُنكَرِ وَٱصۡبِرۡ عَلَىٰ مَآ أَصَابَكَۖ إِنَّ ذَٰلِكَ مِنۡ عَزۡمِ ٱلۡأُمُورِ
31:17.en: O my dear son! Establish worship and enjoin kindness and forbid iniquity, and persevere whatever may befall thee. Lo! that is of the steadfast heart of things

93:11.en: Therefor of the bounty of thy Lord be thy discourse

24:12.ar: لَّوۡلَآ إِذۡ سَمِعۡتُمُوهُ ظَنَّ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنُونَ وَٱلۡمُؤۡمِنَٰتُ بِأَنفُسِهِمۡ خَيۡرࣰ ا وَقَالُواْ هَٰذَآ إِفۡكࣱ مُّبِينࣱ‏
24:12.en: Why did not the believers, men and women, when ye heard it, think good of their own own folk, and say: It is a manifest untruth

43:81.ar: قُلۡ إِن كَانَ لِلرَّحۡمَٰنِ وَلَدࣱ فَأَنَا۠ أَوَّلُ ٱلۡعَٰبِدِينَ
43:81.en: Say (O Muhammad): If the Beneficent One hath a son, then, I shall be first among the worshippers. (But there is no son)

53:23.ar: إِنۡ هِيَ إِلَّآ أَسۡمَآءࣱ سَمَّيۡتُمُوهَآ أَنتُمۡ وَءَابَآؤُكُم مَّآ أَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ بِهَا مِن سُلۡطَٰنٍۚ إِن يَتَّبِعُونَ إِلَّا ٱلظَّنَّ وَمَا تَهۡوَى ٱلۡأَنفُسُۖ وَلَقَدۡ جَآءَهُم مِّن رَّبِّهِمُ ٱلۡهُدَىٰٓ
53:23.en: They are but names which ye have named, ye and your fathers, for which Allah hath revealed no warrant. They follow but a guess and that which (they) themselves desire. And now the guidance from their Lord hath come unto them

2:111.ar: وَقَالُواْ لَن يَدۡخُلَ ٱلۡجَنَّةَ إِلَّا مَن كَانَ هُودًا أَوۡ نَصَٰرَىٰۗ تِلۡكَ أَمَانِيُّهُمۡۗ قُلۡ هَاتُواْ بُرۡهَٰنَكُمۡ إِن كُنتُمۡ صَٰدِقِينَ
2:111.en: And they say: None entereth paradise unless he be a Jew or a Christian. These are their own desires. Say: Bring your proof (of what ye state) if ye are truthful

96:1.en: Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth

43:9.ar: وَلَئِن سَأَلۡتَهُم مَّنۡ خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضَ لَيَقُولُنَّ خَلَقَهُنَّ ٱلۡعَزِيزُ ٱلۡعَلِيمُ
43:9.en: And if thou (Muhammad) ask them: Who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely answer: The Mighty, the Knower created them

3:135.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ إِذَا فَعَلُواْ فَٰحِشَةً أَوۡ ظَلَمُوٓاْ أَنفُسَهُمۡ ذَكَرُواْ ٱللَّهَ فَٱسۡتَغۡفَرُواْ لِذُنُوبِهِمۡ وَمَن يَغۡفِرُ ٱلذُّنُوبَ إِلَّا ٱللَّهُ وَلَمۡ يُصِرُّواْ عَلَىٰ مَا فَعَلُواْ وَهُمۡ يَعۡلَمُونَ
3:135.en: And those who, when they do an evil thing or wrong themselves, remember Allah and implore forgiveness for their sins - Who forgiveth sins save Allah only? - and will not knowingly repeat (the wrong) they did

4:64.ar: وَمَآ أَرۡسَلۡنَا مِن رَّسُولٍ إِلَّا لِيُطَاعَ بِإِذۡنِ ٱللَّهِۚ وَلَوۡ أَنَّهُمۡ إِذ ظَّلَمُوٓاْ أَنفُسَهُمۡ جَآءُوكَ فَٱسۡتَغۡفَرُواْ ٱللَّهَ وَٱسۡتَغۡفَرَ لَهُمُ ٱلرَّسُولُ لَوَجَدُواْ ٱللَّهَ تَوَّابࣰ ا رَّحِيمࣰ ا
4:64.en: We sent no messenger save that he should be obeyed by Allah's leave. And if, when they had wronged themselves, they had but come unto thee and asked forgiveness of Allah, and asked forgiveness of the messenger, they would have found Allah Forgiving, Merciful

PCNMtx9EVCk.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Luqman (Verses 13-17)
PCNMtx9EVCk.one_line: Luqman's counsel as a lesson in gratitude: shirk as injustice, honouring parents without self-interest, the mustard seed, and holding on to prayer.
PCNMtx9EVCk.summary: He frames all of Luqman's counsel to his son as teaching a life of gratitude. Praise is the inner recognition that Allah deserves all credit; gratitude is the action that repays a favour, and turning the spotlight from oneself to Allah cures vanity and arrogance. Shirk is the first breach of gratitude because it puts worship where it does not belong. The two verses on parents are Allah's own words inserted into Luqman's speech, because a father commanding his son to honour him would be a conflict of interest. From this he draws a wide rule: never use religion to demand what benefits you, as rulers do with obedience or spouses with hadith, and he points to the Prophet's silence during the slander of Aishah. Parents must make honouring them easy. The phrase about following what you have no knowledge of shows the Quran never asks for blind following, and he criticises late anti-intellectual trends. Shirk appeals because many sources of authority let people escape a single law. He explains the mustard seed image and the names al-Latif and al-Khabir, stresses that prayer must never be abandoned, and notes that Luqman omits zakat because the boy has no money: teaching must address what the listener actually needs.

outline.heading: Luqman's gentle admonition and a life of gratitude
outline.gist: Admonition must be tender; Luqman lived a life of gratitude, and every hardship borne patiently becomes something to thank Allah for.

outline.heading: The difference between praise and gratitude
outline.gist: Hamd is recognising that Allah deserves credit for all good; shukr is the action that repays a favour, and it flows from hamd.

outline.heading: Gratitude expressed through giving
outline.gist: Gratitude means passing blessings on, as the Prophet did before prophethood by carrying burdens and helping the needy.

outline.heading: Praise as a spotlight that cures vanity and pride
outline.gist: The Prophet was named for praise; shining the spotlight on Allah instead of the self removes vanity and arrogance, which always come together.

outline.heading: Shirk as placing worship where it does not belong
outline.gist: Injustice means putting a thing out of place; shirk wrongs oneself and Allah's rightful station.

outline.heading: The parents verses are Allah's words, not Luqman's
outline.gist: Luqman gives five admonitions; the two verses between them are Allah's interjection.

outline.heading: Why Luqman did not tell his son to honour him
outline.gist: Commanding what benefits you personally is a conflict of interest; parents should not order children to honour them.

outline.heading: Honouring parents outlives them
outline.gist: Birr ends with your death, not theirs; likewise a scholar should not command people to revere scholars.

outline.heading: Rulers and husbands who exploit religious commands
outline.gist: Dictators inflate obedience to those in authority; a husband should not preach obedience to his wife.

outline.heading: The Prophet's silence during the slander of Aishah
outline.gist: Though he held religious and political authority, he waited a month for revelation rather than act in his own interest.

outline.heading: Build relationships that produce honour naturally
outline.gist: Let others do the preaching; build ties with children and spouse so goodness comes without trading hadith.

outline.heading: People only accept sincere advice
outline.gist: Once people sense the adviser benefits, they stop trusting him.

outline.heading: Allah commands honouring parents: weakness upon weakness
outline.gist: The mother's exhausting pregnancy and two years of nursing; thank Allah and then your parents, and know you will be asked.

outline.heading: If parents strive to make you commit shirk
outline.gist: The verse imagines parents using every effort to push the very thing Luqman warned against.

outline.heading: What you have no knowledge of: nothing followed blindly
outline.gist: Even rejecting shirk must rest on knowledge; scholars followed texts by examining evidence and purposes.

outline.heading: The Quran demands proof and thought
outline.gist: No religious book commands reflection like the Quran; whoever tells you to shut your mind has an agenda and no argument.

outline.heading: Anti-intellectualism is a late development
outline.gist: Banning philosophy and inquiry arose in the age of decline; a strong idea fears no comparison.

outline.heading: Know your own foundations first
outline.gist: Young people and new Muslims should build a base in their religion before diving into opposing thought.

outline.heading: Accompany them in this world with kindness
outline.gist: Do not obey parents in shirk, yet keep good company with them; ma'ruf is whatever people recognise as good.

outline.heading: Follow the way of those who turn to Allah
outline.gist: Stay on the path of the prophets and righteous; all return to Allah who will inform them of their deeds.

outline.heading: You answer for your own honouring
outline.gist: You are judged on your birr, they on their conduct; cutting off parents over money or favouritism is unacceptable.

outline.heading: Parents must make honouring easy
outline.gist: From his counselling: a father calls a dutiful son disobedient because nothing satisfies him.

outline.heading: See yourself as commanded, not as a recipient
outline.gist: Read religion as duties on you; a scholar who calls himself a scholar has made himself a receiver of honour.

outline.heading: Back to Luqman: the mustard seed and the commands
outline.gist: Allah mentions the return twice so the duty to parents is not forgotten; recitation of the next two verses.

outline.heading: The first admonition is creedal
outline.gist: All counsel falls under gratitude, and its first item concerns belief; the next verse gives the reason.

outline.heading: The mustard seed: language and smallness
outline.gist: Notes on the conditional form, cited from al-Zamakhshari and al-Biqa'i; the mustard seed is the smallest thing the Arabs knew.

outline.heading: Hidden in a rock, the heavens or the earth
outline.gist: Weightless and hidden, Allah still brings it out; nothing is lost.

outline.heading: Al-Latif and al-Khabir
outline.gist: Al-Latif knows the finest details and is gentle with His servants; al-Khabir knows what is hidden in souls; names with two meanings are loved.

outline.heading: Why equate a creature with the Creator?
outline.gist: No partner has this power; the Arabs admitted Allah created the heavens yet assigned partners for rain, children and war.

outline.heading: Shirk multiplies sources of authority
outline.gist: Like a child playing parents off each other, people prefer many decision-makers; homes, countries and companies collapse without one.

outline.heading: Shirk as a way around Allah's law
outline.gist: Partners let desires pass with a sacrifice or a bought pardon; only Allah forgives sins.

outline.heading: Shirk in Luqman's day and ours
outline.gist: Shirk was profitable and corrupts the fitrah and reason; some of it has crept into Muslim lands.

outline.heading: Establish the prayer: never cut the rope
outline.gist: However far you stray, keep praying; it is your living relationship with Allah.

outline.heading: How seriously scholars treat abandoning prayer
outline.gist: Some schools judged abandoning prayer as disbelief, unlike other pillars; he does not hold this view but cites it to show its weight.

outline.heading: Why Luqman omits zakat: teach what the listener needs
outline.gist: Commands are creedal, ritual, social, moral and purifying, but not financial because the boy has no money; preaching must touch people's real concerns.

outline.heading: Outro

ocbbp-5ZGJk.speaker_note: Says this is the seventh khutbah of his own series and speaks in one voice throughout.
ocbbp-5ZGJk.title: The Quran's Outcomes for Character: Oppression and Ignorance
ocbbp-5ZGJk.one_line: On Al-Ahzab 72: humans are by nature oppressive and ignorant, and the antidotes are standing for justice and seeking knowledge.
ocbbp-5ZGJk.summary: He takes the two biggest traits in his character series, zulm and jahl, from the verse where man alone accepted the amanah and was called zaluman jahulan. He reads amanah either as free will, which sets humans apart from everything but the jinn, or as the pinnacle of ethics, trustworthiness, which is honesty put into action and the reason Quraysh accepted the Prophet as arbiter when rebuilding the Kaaba. Oppression is mentioned 289 times; Islam exists to oppose it, and anti-oppression is a principle distinct from justice because even when you cannot tell what is just, you can see oppression and refuse it. Allah forbade oppression on Himself. Everyone has a monster that would love to oppress and needs only opportunity; the holy land shows people who were oppressed becoming oppressors once given power, and Muslims should assume the same tendency in themselves. Ignorance is a poison: add it to wealth, science, religion or politics and the result is evil. The antidotes, pursuing justice against yourself first and seeking knowledge, both appear in the first revelation, where 'read' means learning from life, the clot of blood reminds the aggressive human of his weakness, and man transgresses when he feels self-sufficient.

outline.heading: Opening
The two largest traits: oppression and ignorance
outline.gist: He has chosen the two largest character topics in the Quran, which cannot be covered in depth, only pointed to. Oppression is mentioned 289 times and opposing it is the essence of why Islam was sent; the era before Islam is named for ignorance, the enemy of all good and the root of every evil.

outline.heading: Al-Ahzab 72: the amanah as free will
outline.gist: One of the most famous verses, which scholars still debate: We offered the amanah. Understood as the ability to choose freely, it is what sets the human apart from every creation except the jinn.

outline.heading: The amanah as trustworthiness: al-Amin at the Kaaba
outline.gist: Or the amanah is the pinnacle of ethics. When Quraysh, on the brink of civil war over rebuilding the Kaaba, agreed to accept whoever came through the gate, they rejoiced that it was the trustworthy one. Trustworthiness is honesty translated into action.

outline.heading: The heavens refused; man accepted
outline.gist: The heavens, earth and mountains, beyond our power to control, were offered the choice to obey or disobey and refused out of fear of the risk; the human accepted. It was not a meeting you missed but a description of human nature: no other creature was equipped to choose.

outline.heading: Know your nature and you are ahead
outline.gist: The Quran's negative traits are not for shame but for understanding. If you know you tend to oppress and to be ignorant, you are ahead of the game. Every other creature is stunned that humans can say no to the King of Kings; that was the gift they were given.

outline.heading: Anti-oppression, a principle of its own
outline.gist: Zalum is an intensive form: it happens again and again, and the Quran speaks of nothing as much as oppression. Justice and righteousness are one thing, being anti-oppression another: a judge who cannot tell what is just can still refuse to oppress. Allah says He has forbidden oppression on Himself and among His servants, so do not oppress one another.

outline.heading: The monster inside: all it takes is opportunity
outline.gist: Seven weeks into these traits: are they avoidable? Of course, but not at first. People carry a monster that would love to oppress; unless they tame it and change how they think about equality and rights, all it takes is the upper hand for it to show.

outline.heading: The holy land: the oppressed turned oppressors
outline.gist: It takes great ethics to be oppressed, be given power, and not oppress. The people who cried to the world that they were oppressed were given land and now oppress. Only Quranic transformation of character prevents it, and Muslims must assume the same tendency in themselves.

outline.heading: Jahul: ignorance poisons everything
outline.gist: Our biggest difficulty is not knowing the future; knowing it would end life's joy and motivation, but not knowing is hard. Mix ignorance with anything and the result is evil: wealth, science, religion or politics with ignorance give what we watch every day.

outline.heading: The two antidotes: justice and knowledge
outline.gist: The human must pursue justice, accepting it on himself before others, refusing to oppress or let oppression pass anywhere without standing against it, and must keep seeking knowledge. These two are far more powerful than Muslims realize.

outline.heading: Iqra: read your life
outline.gist: Both antidotes are in the first revelation. Iqra is not reciting the written word; its five or six meanings come down to learning, gaining experience, gathering and critically processing information and benefiting from others' wisdom, as in 'read your life'. The command has no object.

outline.heading: The clot of blood: remember how weak you are
outline.gist: In the name of your Lord who created man from a clot: the aggressive, oppressive human is reminded he was a tiny piece of blood that could have been lost if his mother sneezed too hard. Read, and your Lord is the most generous.

outline.heading: Man transgresses when he feels self-sufficient
outline.gist: Tughyan is oppression made systematic, a chosen way of life rather than a one-off mistake. It appears once man sees himself as needing nothing, no people and not Allah, until the Quran changes him.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.note: Zulm is the most discussed subject in the Quran and opposing it is why Islam was sent. Anti-oppression is a principle of its own: you can always identify oppression even when justice is unclear. Allah forbade it on Himself; humans carry a monster that oppresses once given the upper hand.

themes.note: Ignorance is the root of all evil; mixed with wealth, science, religion or politics it produces what we see today. Seeking knowledge is its only antidote, and iqra in the first revelation means lifelong learning, critical processing of experience and reading your own life.

31:16.ar: يَٰبُنَيَّ إِنَّهَآ إِن تَكُ مِثۡقَالَ حَبَّةࣲ مِّنۡ خَرۡدَلࣲ فَتَكُن فِي صَخۡرَةٍ أَوۡ فِي ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ أَوۡ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ يَأۡتِ بِهَا ٱللَّهُۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَطِيفٌ خَبِيرࣱ‏
31:16.en: O my dear son! Lo! though it be but the weight of a grain of mustard-seed, and though it be in a rock, or in the heavens, or in the earth, Allah will bring it forth. Lo! Allah is Subtile, Aware

31:17.ar: يَٰبُنَيَّ أَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَأۡمُرۡ بِٱلۡمَعۡرُوفِ وَٱنۡهَ عَنِ ٱلۡمُنكَرِ وَٱصۡبِرۡ عَلَىٰ مَآ أَصَابَكَۖ إِنَّ ذَٰلِكَ مِنۡ عَزۡمِ ٱلۡأُمُورِ
31:17.en: O my dear son! Establish worship and enjoin kindness and forbid iniquity, and persevere whatever may befall thee. Lo! that is of the steadfast heart of things

31:18.ar: وَلَا تُصَعِّرۡ خَدَّكَ لِلنَّاسِ وَلَا تَمۡشِ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ مَرَحًاۖ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ كُلَّ مُخۡتَالࣲ فَخُورࣲ‏
31:18.en: Turn not thy cheek in scorn toward folk, nor walk with pertness in the land. Lo! Allah loveth not each braggart boaster

31:19.ar: وَٱقۡصِدۡ فِي مَشۡيِكَ وَٱغۡضُضۡ مِن صَوۡتِكَۚ إِنَّ أَنكَرَ ٱلۡأَصۡوَٰتِ لَصَوۡتُ ٱلۡحَمِيرِ
31:19.en: Be modest in thy bearing and subdue thy voice. Lo! the harshest of all voices is the voice of the ass

31:13.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ لُقۡمَٰنُ لِٱبۡنِهِۦ وَهُوَ يَعِظُهُۥ يَٰبُنَيَّ لَا تُشۡرِكۡ بِٱللَّهِۖ إِنَّ ٱلشِّرۡكَ لَظُلۡمٌ عَظِيمࣱ‏
31:13.en: And (remember) when Luqman said unto his son, when he was exhorting him: O my dear son! Ascribe no partners unto Allah. Lo! to ascribe partners (unto Him) is a tremendous wrong

2:229.ar: ٱلطَّلَٰقُ مَرَّتَانِۖ فَإِمۡسَاكُۢ بِمَعۡرُوفٍ أَوۡ تَسۡرِيحُۢ بِإِحۡسَٰنࣲۗ وَلَا يَحِلُّ لَكُمۡ أَن تَأۡخُذُواْ مِمَّآ ءَاتَيۡتُمُوهُنَّ شَيۡـًٔا إِلَّآ أَن يَخَافَآ أَلَّا يُقِيمَا حُدُودَ ٱللَّهِۖ فَإِنۡ خِفۡتُمۡ أَلَّا يُقِيمَا حُدُودَ ٱللَّهِ فَلَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيۡهِمَا فِيمَا ٱفۡتَدَتۡ بِهِۦۗ تِلۡكَ حُدُودُ ٱللَّهِ فَلَا تَعۡتَدُوهَاۚ وَمَن يَتَعَدَّ حُدُودَ ٱللَّهِ فَأُوْلَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلظَّٰلِمُونَ
2:229.en: Divorce must be pronounced twice and then (a woman) must be retained in honour or released in kindness. And it is not lawful for you that ye take from women aught of that which ye have given them; except (in the case) when both fear that they may not be able to keep within the limits (imposed by) Allah. And if ye fear that they may not be able to keep the limits of Allah, in that case it is no sin for either of them if the woman ransom herself. These are the limits (imposed by) Allah. Transgress them not. For whoso transgresseth Allah's limits: such are wrong-doers

19:16.ar: وَٱذۡكُرۡ فِي ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ مَرۡيَمَ إِذِ ٱنتَبَذَتۡ مِنۡ أَهۡلِهَا مَكَانࣰ ا شَرۡقِيࣰّ ا
19:16.en: And make mention of Mary in the Scripture, when she had withdrawn from her people to a chamber looking East

5:72.ar: لَقَدۡ كَفَرَ ٱلَّذِينَ قَالُوٓاْ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ ٱلۡمَسِيحُ ٱبۡنُ مَرۡيَمَۖ وَقَالَ ٱلۡمَسِيحُ يَٰبَنِيٓ إِسۡرَٰٓءِيلَ ٱعۡبُدُواْ ٱللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمۡۖ إِنَّهُۥ مَن يُشۡرِكۡ بِٱللَّهِ فَقَدۡ حَرَّمَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَيۡهِ ٱلۡجَنَّةَ وَمَأۡوَىٰهُ ٱلنَّارُۖ وَمَا لِلظَّٰلِمِينَ مِنۡ أَنصَارࣲ‏
5:72.en: They surely disbelieve who say: Lo! Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary. The Messiah (himself) said: O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord. Lo! whoso ascribeth partners unto Allah, for him Allah hath forbidden paradise. His abode is the Fire. For evil-doers there will be no helpers

17:23.ar: ۞وَقَضَىٰ رَبُّكَ أَلَّا تَعۡبُدُوٓاْ إِلَّآ إِيَّاهُ وَبِٱلۡوَٰلِدَيۡنِ إِحۡسَٰنًاۚ إِمَّا يَبۡلُغَنَّ عِندَكَ ٱلۡكِبَرَ أَحَدُهُمَآ أَوۡ كِلَاهُمَا فَلَا تَقُل لَّهُمَآ أُفࣲّ وَلَا تَنۡهَرۡهُمَا وَقُل لَّهُمَا قَوۡلࣰ ا كَرِيمࣰ ا
17:23.en: Thy Lord hath decreed, that ye worship none save Him, and (that ye show) kindness to parents. If one of them or both of them attain old age with thee, say not "Fie" unto them nor repulse them, but speak unto them a gracious word

31:12.ar: وَلَقَدۡ ءَاتَيۡنَا لُقۡمَٰنَ ٱلۡحِكۡمَةَ أَنِ ٱشۡكُرۡ لِلَّهِۚ وَمَن يَشۡكُرۡ فَإِنَّمَا يَشۡكُرُ لِنَفۡسِهِۦۖ وَمَن كَفَرَ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَنِيٌّ حَمِيدࣱ‏
31:12.en: And verily We gave Luqman wisdom, saying: Give thanks unto Allah; and whosoever giveth thanks, he giveth thanks for (the good of) his soul. And whosoever refuseth - Lo! Allah is Absolute, Owner of Praise

11:88.ar: قَالَ يَٰقَوۡمِ أَرَءَيۡتُمۡ إِن كُنتُ عَلَىٰ بَيِّنَةࣲ مِّن رَّبِّي وَرَزَقَنِي مِنۡهُ رِزۡقًا حَسَنࣰ اۚ وَمَآ أُرِيدُ أَنۡ أُخَالِفَكُمۡ إِلَىٰ مَآ أَنۡهَىٰكُمۡ عَنۡهُۚ إِنۡ أُرِيدُ إِلَّا ٱلۡإِصۡلَٰحَ مَا ٱسۡتَطَعۡتُۚ وَمَا تَوۡفِيقِيٓ إِلَّا بِٱللَّهِۚ عَلَيۡهِ تَوَكَّلۡتُ وَإِلَيۡهِ أُنِيبُ
11:88.en: He said: O my people! Bethink you: if I am (acting) on a clear proof from my Lord and He sustaineth me with fair sustenance from Him (how can I concede aught to you)? I desire not to do behind your backs that which I ask you not to do. I desire naught save reform so far as I am able. My welfare is only in Allah. In Him I trust and unto Him I turn (repentant)

26:17.en: (Saying): Let the Children of Israel go with us

17:37.ar: وَلَا تَمۡشِ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ مَرَحًاۖ إِنَّكَ لَن تَخۡرِقَ ٱلۡأَرۡضَ وَلَن تَبۡلُغَ ٱلۡجِبَالَ طُولࣰ ا
17:37.en: And walk not in the earth exultant. Lo! thou canst not rend the earth, nor canst thou stretch to the height of the hills

24:30.ar: قُل لِّلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ يَغُضُّواْ مِنۡ أَبۡصَٰرِهِمۡ وَيَحۡفَظُواْ فُرُوجَهُمۡۚ ذَٰلِكَ أَزۡكَىٰ لَهُمۡۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ خَبِيرُۢ بِمَا يَصۡنَعُونَ
24:30.en: Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and be modest. That is purer for them. Lo! Allah is aware of what they do

sgeaDaoysbE.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Luqman (Verses 17-19)
sgeaDaoysbE.one_line: Luqman's remaining counsel: enjoining good as social work for youth in Canada, patience as true strength, humility, manners and a gentle joke.
sgeaDaoysbE.summary: He opens with a principle of teaching: the speaker must dwell on what his audience needs, or young people feel religion has nothing to do with them, and Luqman chose his son's topics with that wisdom. Enjoining good and forbidding evil are social terms, rooted in what a society already recognises as good or bad, while reform (islah) is the prophetic work of changing customs that anger Allah. Muslims in Canada should work with their neighbours on shared values, joining charities, rights and environmental groups, so that their call to reform elsewhere is heard; he contrasts this with Muslim absence from a hospital donor wall and Muslim names in local criminal cases. Patience is perseverance in action, and it is where a young man should prove his strength, unlike the pre-Islamic boast of violence. The fifth counsel targets arrogance and vanity, the two great diseases of the heart, which he links to racism and to the hadith barring the proud from paradise. The sixth teaches manners, which make a child loved and open doors for him, and the closing image of the donkey's voice shows Luqman lightening serious advice with humour. Parents should copy this curriculum.

outline.heading: Dwell on what the audience needs
outline.gist: A teacher lengthens or shortens according to people's needs; preaching irrelevant topics drives youth away from religion.

outline.heading: Fitting verses to the occasion
outline.gist: Do not recite divorce verses at a wedding; Ja'far recited the story of Maryam before the Negus; cutting texts for agendas is distortion.

outline.heading: Why he teaches the whole Quran in order
outline.gist: Every surah is needed, so he does not pick short courses, but he spends longer on verses that touch present life.

outline.heading: What should Luqman counsel his son about?
outline.gist: Luqman addressed his son's actual needs; Islamic discourse often feels aimed at aliens because it ignores young people's struggles.

outline.heading: Wrong priorities: the haircut and the hashish
outline.gist: A mother upset by her son's haircut while he has been using hashish daily for three years.

outline.heading: Shirk then, economic servitude now
outline.gist: Shirk was a system for controlling people; today jobs, debts and taxes enslave people and silence them.

outline.heading: Recap: the reasoned creed, prayer, and no zakat
outline.gist: Luqman explains why shirk is wrong, commands prayer, and skips zakat because the boy has no money; teach him not to waste money instead.

outline.heading: Ma'ruf and munkar are social, not legal terms
outline.gist: Halal, haram and prayer are fiqh terms; ma'ruf and munkar take their meaning from what society knows.

outline.heading: Custom is authoritative within the shariah
outline.gist: The legal maxim that custom carries weight unless it crosses Allah's limits; dawah begins where custom conflicts.

outline.heading: What Canadian society already deems good and bad
outline.gist: Canadians frown on drugs and heavy drinking and value courtesy, queuing and patient driving; these we enjoin with them.

outline.heading: Reform is the prophets' mission
outline.gist: Islah is examining a people's customs and changing what angers Allah, a different task from enjoining shared good.

outline.heading: Youth need a role in community work
outline.gist: Luqman makes his son socially active; newcomer youth often live in Canada without feeling part of it.

outline.heading: Religious police confused the concept
outline.gist: A committee that beat people for its own reading of the law made people think enjoining good means policing halal and haram.

outline.heading: Prophets reformed specific wrongs and kept good values
outline.gist: Shu'ayb sought only reform; Moses challenged the enslavement of the Israelites; the Prophet perfected Arab virtues and fought specific evils.

outline.heading: A rooted generation can challenge society
outline.gist: Young Muslims confident in their identity and part of society can enjoin its good and then credibly call for reform; we are one society.

outline.heading: Why our objections are not heard
outline.gist: If we do not support shared values, our stand on gender and sexuality looks like rejecting everything about them.

outline.heading: No Muslim names on the hospital donor wall
outline.gist: At the hospital where he works, hundreds of donors and no Muslim foundation, though Muslims rely on free healthcare.

outline.heading: A Muslim judge in tears over trafficking cases
outline.gist: A veteran judge showed him that the accused in local human trafficking cases carried Muslim names.

outline.heading: Neutrality on shared good is wrong
outline.gist: Enjoin society's good and forbid its evil unless it conflicts with the shariah; that conflict is the field of reform.

outline.heading: Each prophet's field of reform
outline.gist: Shu'ayb reformed cheating in trade, Moses political oppression, Lot moral corruption; Luqman gives his son the simpler task.

outline.heading: Join organisations that do good
outline.gist: Youth should volunteer in human rights, animal welfare, environmental and anti-drug groups; it builds confidence and voice.

outline.heading: Shared evils and reforming ourselves first
outline.gist: Everyone condemns domestic abuse, yet Muslims rank high in it; we must reform ourselves before calling others.

outline.heading: Patience means persevering in action
outline.gist: Sabr is not waiting or sitting but continuing good work under hardship, like climbing a mountain at night in winter.

outline.heading: Patience is where a young man proves strength
outline.gist: Strength is not fists or muscles but enduring calamity without losing faith, family or character.

outline.heading: Pre-Islamic strength versus prophetic strength
outline.gist: The boastful verses of Amr ibn Kulthum against the Prophet's teaching that the strong one controls himself in anger.

outline.heading: Recitation of the last two verses
outline.gist: Recitation and articulation notes on the closing verses of Luqman's counsel.

outline.heading: Fifth counsel is purification: when to learn tazkiyah
outline.gist: Years ago a scholar told him the science of the heart should be learned first, citing this very verse.

outline.heading: Do not turn your cheek away from people
outline.gist: Turning the cheek is the arrogant person's way of making others feel unwelcome.

outline.heading: Do not walk the earth in self-praise
outline.gist: Marah means seeing oneself as deserving praise, the centre of the universe; Allah does not love the arrogant boaster.

outline.heading: Arrogance and vanity: the two great diseases
outline.gist: The mukhtal looks down on people and the fakhur admires himself; few are ever freed of these.

outline.heading: Praiseworthy dignity and the turning of fortune
outline.gist: Honour is good only after submitting to Allah; whoever looks down on people today may be beneath them tomorrow.

outline.heading: Racism is generalised arrogance
outline.gist: Racism is pride extended to a whole race, nation or religion; you will not pierce the earth or reach the mountains.

outline.heading: Pride bars from paradise and loses Allah's love
outline.gist: The authentic hadith on an atom's weight of pride; how can anyone accept a station where Allah does not love him?

outline.heading: Teach children to examine their feelings
outline.gist: Parents must help children ask why they love, hate or envy, because untreated diseases of the heart grow.

outline.heading: Sixth counsel: manners make your child loved
outline.gist: Anyone loves his own children; the skill is making others love them, and polite children have doors opened for them.

outline.heading: Moderate your walk and lower your voice
outline.gist: Neither rushing and clumsy nor hiding shyly; speak neither loudly nor too faintly.

outline.heading: Luqman's joke: the donkey's voice
outline.gist: Children need lightness; the Prophet often joked, and Luqman ends his counsel with a gentle humorous image.

outline.heading: A child's manners reflect his upbringing
outline.gist: An impolite child is not to blame; al-Ma'arri's peacock verses on children imitating their parents.

outline.heading: Luqman's six counsels as a curriculum
outline.gist: Creed with reasons, ritual, social, personal, purification and manners, then a joke; the ritual command is the shortest.

outline.heading: Prayer is empty without knowing Allah
outline.gist: There is no benefit in prayer if the child does not understand who Allah is or how to live among people.

29:45.ar: ٱتۡلُ مَآ أُوحِيَ إِلَيۡكَ مِنَ ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ وَأَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَۖ إِنَّ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ تَنۡهَىٰ عَنِ ٱلۡفَحۡشَآءِ وَٱلۡمُنكَرِۗ وَلَذِكۡرُ ٱللَّهِ أَكۡبَرُۗ وَٱللَّهُ يَعۡلَمُ مَا تَصۡنَعُونَ
29:45.en: Recite that which hath been inspired in thee of the Scripture, and establish worship. Lo! worship preserveth from lewdness and iniquity, but verily remembrance of Allah is more important. And Allah knoweth what ye do

3:35.ar: إِذۡ قَالَتِ ٱمۡرَأَتُ عِمۡرَٰنَ رَبِّ إِنِّي نَذَرۡتُ لَكَ مَا فِي بَطۡنِي مُحَرَّرࣰ ا فَتَقَبَّلۡ مِنِّيٓۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلۡعَلِيمُ
3:35.en: (Remember) when the wife of 'Imran said: My Lord! I have vowed unto Thee that which is in my belly as a consecrated (offering). Accept it from me. Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Hearer, the Knower

3:36.ar: فَلَمَّا وَضَعَتۡهَا قَالَتۡ رَبِّ إِنِّي وَضَعۡتُهَآ أُنثَىٰ وَٱللَّهُ أَعۡلَمُ بِمَا وَضَعَتۡ وَلَيۡسَ ٱلذَّكَرُ كَٱلۡأُنثَىٰۖ وَإِنِّي سَمَّيۡتُهَا مَرۡيَمَ وَإِنِّيٓ أُعِيذُهَا بِكَ وَذُرِّيَّتَهَا مِنَ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنِ ٱلرَّجِيمِ
3:36.en: And when she was delivered she said: My Lord! Lo! I am delivered of a female - Allah knew best of what she was delivered - the male is not as the female; and lo! I have named her Mary, and lo! I crave Thy protection for her and for her offspring from Satan the outcast

3:37.ar: فَتَقَبَّلَهَا رَبُّهَا بِقَبُولٍ حَسَنࣲ وَأَنۢبَتَهَا نَبَاتًا حَسَنࣰ ا وَكَفَّلَهَا زَكَرِيَّاۖ كُلَّمَا دَخَلَ عَلَيۡهَا زَكَرِيَّا ٱلۡمِحۡرَابَ وَجَدَ عِندَهَا رِزۡقࣰ اۖ قَالَ يَٰمَرۡيَمُ أَنَّىٰ لَكِ هَٰذَاۖ قَالَتۡ هُوَ مِنۡ عِندِ ٱللَّهِۖ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَرۡزُقُ مَن يَشَآءُ بِغَيۡرِ حِسَابٍ
3:37.en: And her Lord accepted her with full acceptance and vouchsafed to her a goodly growth; and made Zachariah her guardian. Whenever Zachariah went into the sanctuary where she was, he found that she had food. He said: O Mary! Whence cometh unto thee this (food)? She answered: It is from Allah. Allah giveth without stint to whom He will

ESPchfQehPM.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah: The Rituals, Episode 20
ESPchfQehPM.one_line: The two prostrations as a conversation with Allah, how to ask in dua, the sitting for forgiveness that cures arrogance, and congregation curing envy.
ESPchfQehPM.summary: Rituals define a religion, and salah only restrains indecency when it is understood and practised well, so adults must re-examine the prayer they learned mechanically as children. After reviewing the first three postures, he explains that the two prostrations give two chances to ask, for the present and the future. The first half shapes the asking: guidance tells you what to want and even to ask to stop wanting things you should not; magnification means asking boldly from Allah's generosity rather than one's own merit; gratitude removes the disgruntled tone. Dua is not a genie's lamp but a conversation that documents your values, answered in many forms, as Maryam's mother, Ayyub and Ya'qub show. No one but Allah truly wants to hear our complaints, so complain to Him, not about Him. Speaking to Him in your raw form, without social masks, is what produces khushoo; the companions, rough desert men, wept freely in dua yet carried the world. The sitting between prostrations is for forgiveness: keep a specific sin in mind, one each week, and the awareness of your own sins cures arrogance. The tashahhud closes each meeting, and praying as part of a congregation cures envy, so salah done well treats every disease of the heart.

outline.heading: Rituals define the religion
outline.gist: Salah restrains indecency and wrongdoing only when it is properly understood and practised, not automatically.

outline.heading: Re-examine what you inherited
outline.gist: At the age of reason revisit inherited beliefs, judgments and habits, including the mechanical salah learned as a child, until it becomes a sanctuary.

outline.heading: Review: the three offerings
outline.gist: Standing to embrace His guidance after a pause, bowing to magnify Him, and rising to praise Him even when nothing comes to mind.

outline.heading: Two prostrations: a second chance to ask
outline.gist: The second sujud is a follow-up for what you forgot, like the narration of Allah reminding a servant of things he did not ask for; use them for present and future.

outline.heading: Guidance shapes what you ask for
outline.gist: If you asked for guidance, your requests should reflect your purpose; when you crave fame and wealth, ask Allah to free you of the craving.

outline.heading: Never ask for what is haram
outline.gist: Asking Allah to help you sin is mockery or confusion; you ask to become better, and guidance defines what better means.

outline.heading: Ask from His generosity, not your merit
outline.gist: If all creation asked and received everything, it would diminish His dominion no more than a needle dipped in the sea; so ask greedily of His generosity.

outline.heading: Ask with gratitude, not disgruntlement
outline.gist: The grateful asker is content with whatever is chosen; the impatient one keeps counting how long he has knocked.

outline.heading: Dua is a conversation, not a genie's lamp
outline.gist: What you ask for documents your values and priorities before Allah; treating dua as instant wish-granting leads to frustration.

outline.heading: The many ways dua is answered
outline.gist: What you asked, at another time, something better, a harm averted, or reward stored; certainty of a response is a condition of dua.

outline.heading: When something is not written for you
outline.gist: A person who asks all their life for children to raise as good Muslims may not receive them but meets Allah with the reward of that intention.

outline.heading: The mother of Maryam talks to her Lord
outline.gist: She told Allah she bore a girl though He knew, named her and sought refuge for her; this is dua as conversation.

outline.heading: Ayyub's restrained dua
outline.gist: After decades of ease and years of illness and loss, he was too shy to ask for relief and only said harm had touched him and Allah is the most merciful.

outline.heading: Dua in your own words
outline.gist: Use the Prophet's and Quranic duas, but also learn to express your inner struggles in your own language.

outline.heading: No one else wants to hear your complaints
outline.gist: People listen out of compassion or duty; only Allah wants you to speak to Him as long as you need, so do not depend on others before Him.

outline.heading: Ya'qub takes his grief to Allah alone
outline.gist: Frustrated by his grief for Yusuf and Binyamin, his sons were told he complained only to Allah.

outline.heading: Complain to Him, not about Him
outline.gist: Complaining is innate in us; dua channels it toward Allah instead of against Him.

outline.heading: The exercise: dua in your raw form
outline.gist: Make dua for a few minutes, then again without repeating anything; drop every social role and speak as a frightened, struggling creation.

outline.heading: Khushoo is an outcome, not a technique
outline.gist: It cannot be forced; it follows when everything is in place, especially speaking to Allah as who you truly are.

outline.heading: The rough men of the desert
outline.gist: Men of the sixth century were far tougher than our grandfathers; one was shocked to see the Prophet kiss his grandson, having never kissed any of his ten children.

outline.heading: Tear-marked cheeks
outline.gist: A companion feared by all bore lines down his face from hours of weeping in dua.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr's weeping in prayer
outline.gist: The man who held the ummah together after the Prophet's death rarely led prayer because he sobbed so much his recitation could not be understood.

outline.heading: Roles outside, servanthood inside
outline.gist: No generation expressed emotion before Allah like the companions, yet they wiped their tears and fought and built Medina; they left their roles at the door of salah.

outline.heading: Dua is worship
outline.gist: Dua is where the relationship with Allah comes down; many people have a bad relationship with God, and the quality of dua reveals yours.

outline.heading: Making the second sujud better
outline.gist: Begin with the glorification, ask, then go down again and speak even more sincerely.

outline.heading: The sitting: a posture of regret
outline.gist: Sitting with head lowered mirrors apology; the Prophet would sit long between prostrations repeating the request for forgiveness.

outline.heading: Tip: have a specific sin in mind
outline.gist: Asking forgiveness for nothing in particular is almost rude; recall where you fell short, failed to act or caused harm.

outline.heading: Awareness of your sins cures arrogance
outline.gist: You know a thousand of your own sins and perhaps one of another's, so you cannot see yourself as better; forgiveness keeps this from crushing self-value.

outline.heading: One sin a week
outline.gist: Focus on one sin in the sitting for a week; repeating it five times a day builds an attitude against it.

outline.heading: Do not rush the sitting

outline.heading: Salah done right cures the heart
outline.gist: Performed properly, salah removes aimlessness, vanity, arrogance, ostentation, envy and isolation, which is the whole point of tazkiyah.

y0lt3MUx2R4.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Muddaththir, Part 5: Verses 32-41
y0lt3MUx2R4.one_line: The oath by moon, night and dawn, the Day that levels the playing field, every soul held in pledge, and why only Allah's compassion frees us.
y0lt3MUx2R4.summary: He recaps the surah's design: inner practice for oneself, outer conduct for society, and the core traits that make carrying Islam to others work. After accepting truth and keeping the bigger picture, he extends the second trait to Western freedom reduced to its details, to salah and moon-sighting disputes, and to people who cannot explain Islam in a 45-second elevator pitch. The third core piece is accountability: once any agenda outranks reward and punishment, all is lost. He explains the oath by the moon, the retreating night and the brightening dawn as images of the moment clarity arrives, and the Day as one of the greatest events. Life is not a level field, so do not compare yourself to others; Judgment levels every hand dealt, and more given means more expected. 'Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned' leads him to the roots of behaviour such as temper, to owning one's own destiny, and to letting children face consequences. The exception, the people of the right, shows that no deed can buy eternal bliss; deeds are a show of love hoping for Allah's compassion, not a transaction.

outline.heading: Opening
A Damascus scholar's two-and-a-half-hour lesson after 30 years of exile
outline.gist: A well-known Damascus scholar his father befriended in Medina was finally allowed home after three decades; at his first lesson he chided the restless crowd that he had not spoken for 30 years, taught for two and a half hours, and died a few months later.

outline.heading: Where the surah sits: Islam for yourself and Islam for society
outline.gist: The preceding surahs give the caller knowledge, ethics, spirituality and conduct, then two examples of da'wah, Nuh's and the Prophet's with the jinn; Al-Muzzammil covers what Islam gives you inwardly and Al-Muddaththir how you carry it to society through its seven opening commands.

outline.heading: First core trait recalled: accepting truth unconditionally
outline.gist: Carrying Islam to others only works if you change course the moment something proves right, however long you argued the opposite; Walid instead said what benefited him rather than what he believed.

outline.heading: Second trait recalled: how Western freedom decayed into its details
outline.gist: Obsession with details that hides the bigger picture afflicts every ideology; freedom of thought and speech, a noble ideal Islam shares, shrank into licence, and the Second Amendment, meant to stop the state oppressing people, became a fight that leaves parents afraid every school morning.

outline.heading: Nineteen showed what disbelievers fixate on; believers only grow in faith
outline.gist: Allah named the number to show how disbelievers would ignore a profound surah and argue over why nineteen, while details only increase the believers' faith without hiding the forest.

outline.heading: Learn the details of worship without losing their purpose
outline.gist: Study salah in depth, its sunnahs, obligations and postures, but never let that outrank why it was prescribed, or the community fights over beard length, moon-sighting and the direction of the qibla while lacking basic decency.

outline.heading: Masjids are for youth, not for fights over the 7:45 Isha time
outline.gist: Complaints about noise or how things are run miss that masjids exist for young people to find comfort, guidance and mentorship; he is tired of explaining the fixed Isha time year after year.

outline.heading: The cave sleepers' number, and a question about their dog
outline.gist: The Quran's prime example is the number of the cave sleepers; he recalls a post-Jumuah Q&A in Syria where someone asked what breed of dog they had.

outline.heading: What is your elevator pitch of Islam?
outline.gist: If someone gives you 45 seconds to explain Islam and you list prayer times and zakat rules, you have lost them; zoom out to the right distance and have a clear, passionate answer ready.

outline.heading: The third core piece: accountability, or all is lost
outline.gist: After reciting the next verses he names accountability as the final piece: the moment any agenda matters more than reward and fear of punishment, not something but all is lost and the work has no baraka.

outline.heading: Kalla, then an oath by the moon, the retreating night and the brightening dawn
outline.gist: Kalla rejects the obsession with details; adbara is the night turning its back to leave, and asfara is making something apparent, as a woman whose face is uncovered is called safirah.

outline.heading: Why these images: the desert Arabs waiting for first light
outline.gist: He swears by what surrounds the moment of clarity: for superstitious desert Arabs the night was terrifying, and comfort came with the first beams of morning.

outline.heading: 'Indeed it is one of the greatest': a pronoun too well known to name
outline.gist: A pronoun with no named referent signals something everyone already knows: the Day, one of the great cosmic events, implying others of like scale.

outline.heading: A warning to humankind: advance or lag behind, it is your choice
outline.gist: The Day is a warning to all people; whether you get ahead or fall back is your own decision, and everyone will be ranked somewhere.

outline.heading: Life is not a level field; the Day levels it
outline.gist: The famous and successful are not necessarily the best, because people start from very different places; only on the Day are all variables accounted for and effort weighed against the hand dealt.

outline.heading: Do not be fooled by where you stand
outline.gist: One who turns a million into ten cannot be compared with one who turns nothing into ten thousand; do not grow arrogant or despair, since you barely know your own hand, let alone anyone else's.

outline.heading: Sitting in a masjid on a Friday night is already a good hand
outline.gist: Like staggered Olympic lanes his mother had to explain to him, you cannot see who is truly ahead; hearing and understanding this talk in a North American masjid already puts you near the front.

outline.heading: Don't compare yourself to others: more given means more expected
outline.gist: His teachers drilled this in: the sinner you look down on may be doing better with a bad hand than you with a good one; no one is impressed by someone flaunting his father's cars, and Allah expects more from whom He gave more.

outline.heading: Every soul held in pledge for what it earned: the pawned soul
outline.gist: He recites the next verses and calls this one an Islamic maxim: rahina is a pawned item held until the debt is paid, so the soul is held until its deeds release it.

outline.heading: Kasabat: everything you do, think and say
outline.gist: Kasb covers every action, thought, word and goal; either your deeds free you or they keep you held, and that is the law of life.

outline.heading: Choices grow from thoughts, feelings and company: find what fuels a behaviour
outline.gist: Beliefs, feelings, plans, intentions and environment mix into what you do, which is why he talks about the heart; if you cannot stop a behaviour, ask hard questions about where it comes from.

outline.heading: Losing your temper is no excuse
outline.gist: Men who break things and hit people then plead that they lost their temper, as if that excuses it; controlling it is not easy but it is doable.

outline.heading: You must care about your destiny more than the preacher does
outline.gist: Preachers end up caring about people's fate more than they do, which is unhealthy; you pay for your deeds, so the drive to change must be yours, as Allah told the Prophet not to destroy himself with grief over those who refuse.

outline.heading: Parents cannot care for their children's lives more than they do
outline.gist: Teach and support, but children must make their own choices; accountability and free choice are central to Islam, so stop bailing children out, hold to consequences and let them learn at home before life teaches harder.

outline.heading: Except the people of the right, in gardens asking about the criminals
outline.gist: One group is not held hostage by its deeds: they are in gardens of bliss asking what became of those who broke Allah's laws, because for them it is Allah's mercy, not their deeds, that decides.

outline.heading: What deed could be worth eternal bliss?
outline.gist: A price must match what it buys, and no deed a human can offer equals a soul freed from punishment forever.

outline.heading: Kings pardon for gain, but you have nothing Allah needs
outline.gist: Kings pardon in return for loyalty, wealth or flattering poetry; like a condemned servant whose king already owns more grain, horses and gold, you are desperate to be freed but hold nothing Allah wants.

outline.heading: Deeds earn His compassion: none enters Paradise by his deeds
outline.gist: Good deeds work by making us worthy of Allah's compassion, not by buying Paradise; the Prophet said not even he would enter by his deeds unless Allah enveloped him in mercy.

outline.heading: The man who insisted on entering by his deeds
outline.gist: Told to enter by Allah's mercy, a man demanded entry by his deeds; weighed against the blessing of one eye they were used up, and he took it back.

outline.heading: Deeds are a show of love, hoping He returns it
outline.gist: Treat deeds as a transaction and you are in trouble; they are a show of love offered in hope that Allah answers with His love and frees you.

outline.heading: Carrying Islam is neither a favour nor a transaction
outline.gist: Standing for the truth and keeping the bigger picture are not enough without knowing why: not as a favour to people or to God, nor as deeds that add up, but as love and gratitude.

outline.heading: Hoping to be accepted as a whole, not itemised
outline.gist: If every choice in the book of your life were examined, none of us could defend it; we hope for a broad acceptance with the good and the bad together.

outline.heading: Who could be confident in his deeds when the Prophet was not?
outline.gist: No living person can claim top-notch deeds; if the Prophet did not feel that way, we only try our best so Allah sees us worthy of His love and does not read out our whole book.

outline.heading: Outro

nY7qY-VxBME.title: The Quran's Outcomes for Character: Selfishness and Weakness
nY7qY-VxBME.one_line: Selfishness (shuhh) must be redirected: be selfless now to win the Hereafter, and care for every suffering Muslim, not only those on the news.
nY7qY-VxBME.summary: Selfishness kept humans alive, but the Quran names it as a flaw, saying man would hoard even Allah's mercy out of fear of running out, condemning those who are stingy and spread stinginess, and promising success to whoever is protected from the shuhh of his soul, a trait the Prophet said destroyed earlier nations. His twist is that Islam does not abolish selfishness but redirects it: be selfish about Jannah, which can only be reached by being selfless here, as Jabir's elderly father showed when he refused to give up his place at Uhud. He then confesses the ummah's selective caring through his own life in Syria: Bosnia, Iraq, Gaza watched with mediocre concern until destruction reached his own city and nobody listened. Caring only for yourself does not even work practically; the wheel of destruction eventually reaches you, as it did the Taifa kings of Andalus. Sudan is starving with little coverage, so it dies in silence. The Ansari who put his children to bed hungry and faked a meal in the dark so a guest could eat shows what selflessness looks like. In the second khutbah he asks parents to raise selfless children, rejects the push-and-shove mentality, tests the audience with 'if everyone lived like you, would the world work', and insists ethics must be unconditional.

outline.heading: Al-Isra 100: he would hoard even Allah's mercy
outline.gist: Without selfishness we would not have survived, but not every part of it is positive; some must be censored. If man held the treasuries of Allah's compassion, he would hold most of it back for fear of running out.

outline.heading: The stingy who command stinginess
outline.gist: Man has always been extremely selfish. The Quran mentions those who are stingy and command others to be stingy, twice, and always in a negative context.

outline.heading: Protected from the shuhh of his soul
outline.gist: Whoever is protected from his own soul's selfishness is the successful one. The Prophet warned that shuhh destroyed the nations before, turning them into people who stole from, killed and violated the dignity of one another.

outline.heading: Selfishness is intrinsic and must be regulated
outline.gist: Shuhh is too big a topic for one khutbah; tazkiyah is largely about removing it. None of these traits is wholly negative: without selfishness you starve and cannot care for yourself, but unregulated it turns you into what Allah is not pleased with.

outline.heading: Be selfish about Jannah
outline.gist: Islam feeds your ultimate selfishness: you are not meant to be selfless about Jannah. Reaching it first and at the highest rank is only possible by being fully selfless in this life; that is how Allah set it up.

outline.heading: Jabir and his father: anything but Jannah
outline.gist: Jabir, 21, insisted he should go to Uhud rather than his 78-year-old father with nine daughters, who was excused. They drew lots and the father won; to his sobbing son he said that for anything other than Jannah he would have given way.

outline.heading: Medium-level caring: growing up in Syria
outline.gist: We are selfish about suffering. Growing up in Syria he heard about Bosnia, saw Iraq invaded next door in 2003 and Gaza bombed more times than he can count, and the community's caring was normalized at a medium level. As an idealistic boy he could not see why no one moved the world while weddings and gatherings went on.

outline.heading: Going numb, until the wheel reached him
outline.gist: As a boy he phoned random Baghdad numbers to say he felt for them. Indifference rubbed off and by 21 he was numb, focused on his studies, until the wheel of death and destruction rolled over his own city and country. He wrote one verse: it is fine that you do not listen to me now, because I did not listen to you when my house was in order.

outline.heading: Selective caring is selfishness
outline.gist: Gaza drew two years of care for religious and historical reasons, yet within weeks of the ceasefire people stopped talking about it. Start with those close and widen, but until the suffering of every Muslim, and every human, matters equally, nothing will change; Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Myanmar, China, Somalia, Ethiopia, Libya and Sudan get almost nothing.

outline.heading: Caring only for yourself does not work
outline.gist: Practically, not ethically: if only you and your family matter, the wheel of destruction will still find you, a little later. Caring for others is itself a selfish act, because what you ignore when it happens to others will happen to you ten times over and no one will listen.

outline.heading: Protect your brother to protect yourself
outline.gist: The nafs's selfishness is shortsighted and ignorant; be selfish the right way. Caring for others means someone will care for you. When you let an enemy harm a brother who was your rival, you are not stronger but weaker; you just have not seen it yet.

outline.heading: The Taifa kings of Andalus
outline.gist: Any history shows that those too egocentric to set aside their egos lost everything. The last Muslim kings of Andalus enjoyed watching enemies take down rival kingdoms and fell a few years later; the knowledge, science and civilization of places like Valencia were lost forever through selfishness.

outline.heading: Sudan dies in silence
outline.gist: Sudan's starvation exceeds what we saw in Gaza, but with less media coverage we watch less, care less, and more die in silence. Advocate for Muslims everywhere: their right to live freely and in dignity, to education, ownership, food and life without oppression. He starts with himself; all are guilty.

outline.heading: The magic of true selflessness
outline.gist: When a person decides to drop self-centredness and acts with no interest in recognition, reward or acknowledgement, only because others need it, jaws drop; it is magical.

outline.heading: The Ansari host
outline.gist: On a cold, rainy night a hungry migrant arrived in Medina with nowhere to stay. An Ansari took him home; his wife put their hungry children to sleep, put out the lamp, and they clattered their spoons in the dark so the guest could eat the only food without guilt. The next morning the Prophet told the companions that Allah was amazed at what they had done, with no likening of Allah to us.

outline.heading: The Ansar loved the migrants
outline.gist: The people of Medina loved that migrants came, though there was no housing and families shared homes, and though some migrants were wealthier, closer to the Prophet or more learned. Even in poverty they put others ahead of themselves: those protected from their soul's selfishness are the successful.

outline.heading: Interlude
Selflessness in everything
outline.gist: Unless we learn it, teach it to our children and show it in our own lives, nothing changes. Advocacy is only one avenue: if you truly saw people as equal you would take nothing without making sure everyone gets an equal share. Consumerism and capitalism teach the opposite.

outline.heading: Push and shove: the father who scolds his son
outline.gist: Growing up in the Middle East teaches you that if you do not kick and step on others you never get served. A boy who came home empty-handed because he did not push is told he is weak, and learns to break rules and let everyone drown. He will not argue about it; the Quran refuses that mentality.

outline.heading: The VIP card test
outline.gist: Forget Islam: if everyone lived as you do, would the world work, or are you taking more than you give? A mental VIP card that exempts you from lines and rules means the shuhh in your heart is eating away and will turn you into a monster.

outline.heading: Interlude
Generalize the passion you had for Gaza
outline.gist: People who almost never came to the masjid stood in the cold rain with signs for two years. That passion must reach everyone who suffers, not only those who share your name, country or looks: if it is real it is for everyone; if it is fake it is just yours. Ethics cannot be conditional or convenient.

outline.heading: The Uyghur brother's stories
outline.gist: Now and then someone from a part of the world his congregation rarely represents tells him of their people's suffering, and it shames him. A Uyghur brother's stories still keep him awake: what happened, and how the Muslims around them carried on as if nothing happened.

outline.heading: You could be in their place
outline.gist: Ethics is treating people as you would want to be treated in their position. Never say you could never be there; that confidence is a punishable arrogance. It takes Allah no effort to put any of us in hardship; be thankful He did not, and use the chance to care by overcoming the selfishness inside.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: Selfishness, greed of the soul (shuhh) and selflessness
themes.note: Selfishness is intrinsic and partly necessary, but unregulated it becomes the shuhh that destroyed earlier nations. Islam redirects it: be selfish about Jannah by being selfless in this life; the ummah's selective caring about Muslim suffering is selfishness in disguise.

themes.label: The companions and the early generations
themes.note: Jabir, 21, and his 78-year-old father with nine daughters drew lots for Uhud; the father won and told his sobbing son he would have given him anything except Jannah. Rightly placed selfishness.

themes.label: Palestine, Gaza and the suffering of Muslims
themes.note: Gaza has been bombed more times than he can count and was met with mediocre caring until the last two years; attention collapsed weeks after the ceasefire. Syria, Bosnia, Iraq, Myanmar, China and now a starving Sudan show the same pattern of ignored suffering.

themes.label: Community building, cooperation and the ummah
themes.note: Until every Muslim's suffering, then every human's, matters equally, nothing changes. Start with those closest and widen. Protecting your brother protects you; caring for others is practical self-preservation because destruction eventually reaches the indifferent.

themes.label: Islamic history and civilization
themes.note: The Taifa rulers of Andalus enjoyed watching enemies take down rival Muslim kingdoms and fell a few years later; Valencia's scholarship and civilization were lost forever because of selfishness.

themes.label: The companions and the early generations
themes.note: The Ansari host who faked a meal in the dark so his guest could eat, and the Ansar who loved the migrants despite poverty, a housing shortage and the migrants' greater wealth or knowledge; the verse about preferring others over oneself.

themes.label: Selfishness, greed of the soul (shuhh) and selflessness
themes.note: Selflessness belongs in every area of life, not only advocacy: see others as truly equal, take nothing without ensuring everyone's share, and drop the mental VIP card. Shuhh left unchecked turns people into monsters.

themes.label: Parenting and raising children
themes.note: Children must be taught and shown selflessness. The father who scolds his son for not pushing in line teaches him to break rules and let others drown; the Quran refuses that upbringing.

themes.label: Modernity, secularism, materialism and their effects
themes.note: Consumerism and capitalism train people to take more than they give, and life in the Middle East trains them to step on others to get served; both contradict the Quran.

themes.label: Activism, civic engagement and the path forward
themes.note: People who rarely came to the masjid stood in the rain for Gaza for two years; that passion must be extended to everyone who suffers, not only those who share your name, country or looks.

themes.label: Values, principles and ethics as a system
themes.note: Ethics cannot be conditional or convenient; they must be consistent across the board. His definition: treating people the way you would want to be treated if you were in their position.

themes.label: Humility vs vanity and arrogance
themes.note: Never say 'I would never be in that position'; it is arrogance that is punishable. Allah could put any of us there without effort; be thankful and use what you have to care for others.

takeaways: Do not deny your selfishness; regulate it and aim it at the Hereafter by being selfless in this life.
